candidates.title: Ask RLHF chat models to verbalize a confidence instead of sampling for probabilities
candidates.rule: For short-form factual QA with RLHF-tuned chat models lacking token logprobs, elicit a numeric confidence in the output tokens rather than estimating confidence from repeated samples; verify on your own data for open-weight models like Llama-2-70B-Chat, where gains were inconsistent.
candidates.passage: we find that verbalized confidences emitted as output tokens are typically better-calibrated than the model’s conditional probabilities on the TriviaQA, SciQ, and TruthfulQA benchmarks
candidates.finding: Across Tables 1-5, verbalized confidence prompts cut ECE relative to sampled label probabilities for gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4, claude-1, claude-2; for Llama-2-70b-chat improvements were less consistent across metrics.
candidates.conditions: Short-answer factual recall; correctness judged by LLM semantic-equivalence check; sampled baseline uses n=10 samples; verbalized method needs only one sample (cheaper).
candidates.limitations: Single paper; short-form QA only, no reasoning or long-form tasks; closed models may have changed since 2023; absolute calibration on TruthfulQA remains poor (ECE ~0.2-0.4); AUC sometimes worse than logprobs (e.g., Claude-1 on SciQ).
candidates.validation_test: On your task, compare ECE/Brier/selective-accuracy AUC of a one-sample verbalized-probability prompt against 10-sample answer-frequency confidence, using an LLM equivalence judge for correctness.

candidates.title: Request multiple candidate answers before confidences
candidates.rule: When eliciting verbalized confidences, prompt for the top-2 or top-4 guesses with a probability each and use the top-ranked one, instead of asking for a single guess and probability.
candidates.passage: Among the methods for verbalizing probabilities directly, we observe that generating and evaluating multiple hypotheses improves calibration (see Figure 1 )
candidates.finding: Verb. 1S top-2/top-4 generally show lower ECE than top-1 across models and datasets (e.g., gpt-3.5-turbo SciQ ECE 0.234 -> 0.132 -> 0.065).
candidates.conditions: One-stage prompt asking for k guesses with per-guess probability; extra output tokens cost; benefit varies by metric.
candidates.limitations: Not uniform: on TriviaQA top-4 sometimes worse than top-2; AUC can drop with larger k (gpt-3.5 SciQ AUC 0.766 at k=2 vs 0.763 at k=4; Claude-1 drops); untested beyond short-form QA.
candidates.validation_test: Run k=1,2,4 variants of the same verbalized prompt on a held-out labeled QA set and compare ECE, temperature-scaled ECE, Brier, and selective-accuracy AUC.

candidates.title: Do not add chain-of-thought to improve confidence calibration
candidates.rule: Do not add chain-of-thought prompting solely to improve confidence calibration in short-form factual QA; it did not help and in places hurt.
candidates.passage: Chain-of-thought prompting does not improve verbalized calibration (see Appendix Figure 5 for additional CoT results).
candidates.finding: Verb. 2S CoT had worse ECE than non-CoT verbalized variants for gpt-3.5-turbo (e.g., SciQ 0.323 vs 0.065 for 1S top-4), and Appendix Figure 5 CoT variants showed no consistent ECE gain.
candidates.conditions: CoT variants tested only on gpt-3.5-turbo in the appendix; calibration metrics only, not answer accuracy.
candidates.limitations: Rule concerns calibration, not accuracy, which CoT may still improve; tested on one model and three factual QA sets; reasoning-heavy domains untested.
candidates.validation_test: Compare CoT and non-CoT verbalized-confidence prompts on the same questions, reporting both accuracy and ECE/Brier, to check whether CoT trades calibration for accuracy in your domain.

reason: The paper compares concrete confidence-elicitation prompts across five RLHF models and three QA datasets, yielding actionable prompting rules (verbalized confidence vs sampled probabilities; top-k multi-guess; CoT null result).
